course.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Responsible AI
course.description: Introduces AI concepts, generative AI, evaluation, human oversight, bias, privacy, security and responsible use through practical cross-disciplinary activities.

outcomes.text: Explain core AI concepts, model limitations and the difference between prediction, generation and human judgement.
Use generative AI tools purposefully while documenting prompts, verification and human contribution.
Evaluate AI outputs for factuality, reliability, bias, privacy, security and task fitness.
Identify stakeholders, harms, benefits and governance controls across an AI use case.
Design a human-centered AI workflow with explicit oversight, evaluation and risk controls.

lessons.title: What AI systems do and do not know
objectives: Distinguish common AI task types
Explain why model output is not equivalent to human understanding
lessons.teaching_material: Artificial intelligence is an umbrella term for computational systems that perform tasks such as classification, prediction, ranking, recognition, recommendation and generation. Models learn statistical patterns from data and use those patterns to produce outputs under defined objectives. Their performance depends on data, design, context and evaluation. Fluent output should not be confused with consciousness, intent or guaranteed truth; users must judge whether the system is suitable for the task and verify consequential claims.
lessons.activity: Classify ten familiar AI-enabled products by task type, input, output, likely training signal and what human judgement is still required.

self_check.q: Does a confident AI response prove that the underlying statement is true?
self_check.a: No. Confidence of expression is not evidence; factual claims must be verified against reliable sources or tests.

self_check.q: What determines whether an AI system is fit for a task?
self_check.a: Its measured performance, limitations, context, risk level, data suitability and the consequences of error.

lessons.title: Human-centered AI and appropriate delegation
objectives: Identify tasks suitable for AI assistance
Define meaningful human oversight
lessons.teaching_material: Human-centered AI begins with the human objective, rights and consequences rather than with the availability of a model. Some tasks are low-risk and reversible, while others affect health, education, employment, finance or legal rights and require much stronger controls. Meaningful oversight means a human has the information, authority, time and competence to challenge or override a system. Simply putting a person at the end of an automated process does not create effective oversight if that person cannot detect or correct errors.
lessons.activity: Create a delegation matrix for twelve study or workplace tasks, rating consequence of error, reversibility, verification difficulty and required human oversight.

self_check.q: What makes human oversight meaningful?
self_check.a: The reviewer must be capable, informed, empowered and given enough time to detect, challenge and correct system output.

self_check.q: Why treat high-impact decisions differently?
self_check.a: Errors can materially affect people's rights, opportunities, safety or livelihood, so stronger evidence and controls are justified.

modules.title: Generative AI, Prompting and Workflow Design

lessons.title: How generative models produce outputs
objectives: Describe generation at a conceptual level
Recognize hallucination and context limitations
lessons.teaching_material: Generative language models produce sequences by estimating likely continuations from learned patterns and the supplied context. They can transform, summarize, draft, classify and reason over provided information, but they may also invent details, lose context, reproduce biases or give inconsistent answers. Prompt quality influences output, yet no prompt can guarantee truth. Reliable workflows therefore combine clear instructions with source grounding, structured outputs, independent checks and bounded use cases.
lessons.activity: Ask an AI system to perform the same task with three prompt designs, then compare completeness, unsupported claims, ambiguity and ease of verification.

self_check.q: Can prompt engineering eliminate hallucinations?
self_check.a: No. Better prompts can reduce some errors, but factual verification and system-level controls are still necessary.

self_check.q: What is source grounding?
self_check.a: Constraining or supporting the model with authoritative source material that can be checked against the output.

lessons.title: Prompt design, iteration and documentation
objectives: Write structured prompts
Maintain an auditable AI work log
lessons.teaching_material: A useful prompt specifies the task, audience, constraints, source boundaries, desired format and criteria for success. Complex work is often safer when decomposed into steps such as extract, analyze, draft and verify rather than asking for a final answer in one pass. Documentation matters in academic and professional use: record the tool, date, material supplied, material generated, consequential prompts and what the human changed or verified. Sensitive data should not be entered into unapproved systems merely to improve convenience.
lessons.activity: Design a four-stage AI-assisted research workflow with prompt templates, verification checkpoints, privacy boundaries and an AI contribution log.

self_check.q: Why decompose a complex AI task?
self_check.a: Smaller stages make errors easier to detect, allow targeted verification and reduce hidden assumptions.

self_check.q: What should an AI use log capture?
self_check.a: Enough information to explain how AI contributed, what data was supplied, what outputs mattered and what human checks were performed.

lessons.title: Testing AI outputs
objectives: Define task-specific evaluation criteria
Build a small test set
lessons.teaching_material: AI evaluation must be tied to the intended task. A writing assistant may be judged on instruction following and factual preservation, while a classifier may require accuracy, recall or subgroup analysis. One impressive example is not a test. A small evaluation set should include normal cases, difficult cases, edge cases and known failure modes, with expected results or a defensible scoring rubric. Repeated evaluation matters because model versions, prompts and surrounding tools can change behavior.
lessons.activity: Create a ten-case evaluation set for one AI use case, define pass/fail criteria and record the system's results plus observed failure patterns.

self_check.q: Why is a demo not sufficient evidence of reliability?
self_check.a: A demo shows selected behavior on a small example and may not represent typical, difficult or adversarial cases.

self_check.q: Why include edge cases?
self_check.a: They reveal failure modes that ordinary examples may hide and are often where real-world harm occurs.

lessons.title: Factuality, citations and verification
objectives: Verify AI-generated factual claims
Detect fabricated or mismatched citations
lessons.teaching_material: AI-generated references require verification at the source. A plausible title, author or DOI can be fabricated, and a real paper can be cited for a claim it does not support. Verification should confirm that the source exists, that bibliographic details match, that the relevant passage or data supports the claim, and that the source is suitable for the question. For calculations or code, independent execution or recomputation is often more reliable than asking the same model to check itself.
lessons.activity: Audit an AI-generated answer containing eight factual claims and five references. Produce a table showing verified, unsupported, incorrect and uncertain items.

self_check.q: Is a real citation automatically a supporting citation?
self_check.a: No. The source must actually contain evidence relevant to the specific claim.

self_check.q: What is a good way to verify AI-generated code?
self_check.a: Run it in a controlled environment, inspect outputs and test it against known and edge cases.

lessons.title: Bias, fairness and uneven performance
objectives: Identify sources of AI bias
Evaluate subgroup performance and fairness trade-offs
lessons.teaching_material: Bias can enter through historical data, sampling, labeling, feature selection, objectives, deployment context and feedback loops. A system can have good overall performance while failing badly for a smaller subgroup. Fairness is not a single mathematical property, and different fairness criteria can conflict. Responsible evaluation therefore asks who benefits, who bears errors, whether performance differs across relevant groups and whether the use of the system is justified at all for the decision being made.
lessons.activity: Analyze a fictional admissions model with subgroup error rates and identify which additional evidence, fairness questions and human controls are required before deployment.

self_check.q: Can high overall accuracy hide unfair performance?
self_check.a: Yes. Aggregate metrics can conceal high error rates or systematic disadvantage for smaller groups.

self_check.q: Is there one universal fairness metric?
self_check.a: No. Different definitions reflect different values and can conflict, so context and stakeholder impact matter.

lessons.title: Privacy, security, copyright and confidential data
objectives: Recognize data-exposure risks in AI use
Separate attribution, privacy and permission questions
lessons.teaching_material: AI use can expose information through prompts, uploaded files, logs, integrations or retained conversation history. Users must follow institutional rules for confidential, personal, client or research data and should minimize data shared with external tools. Prompt injection and malicious content can manipulate AI-enabled workflows, particularly when systems can call tools or access files. Copyright and attribution remain separate questions: generated or transformed content may still require rights analysis, source checking and disclosure.
lessons.activity: Threat-model an AI assistant that can read documents and send email; identify sensitive assets, attack paths, required permissions and human approval points.

self_check.q: Why is data minimization relevant to AI prompts?
self_check.a: Providing unnecessary sensitive information increases privacy exposure without improving the legitimate task.

self_check.q: What is prompt injection in broad terms?
self_check.a: Malicious or untrusted content attempts to override intended instructions or cause an AI system to take unsafe actions.

lessons.title: Risk management and governance controls
objectives: Apply a simple AI risk-management cycle
Select controls proportionate to risk
lessons.teaching_material: Responsible AI governance is a lifecycle practice. Teams map context and stakeholders, measure performance and harms, manage identified risks, and govern responsibility, documentation and escalation. Controls may include restricted use cases, approval thresholds, evaluation benchmarks, data controls, logging, user disclosure, fallback procedures and incident response. Risk management is not a document produced once; it should change when the model, data, users, law or deployment environment changes.
lessons.activity: Complete a one-page risk register for an AI use case with stakeholders, harms, likelihood, impact, controls, owner, evidence and review trigger.

self_check.q: Why should controls be proportionate?
self_check.a: Higher-consequence or less-reversible uses justify stronger evidence, oversight and safeguards than low-risk assistive tasks.

self_check.q: When should an AI risk assessment be revisited?
self_check.a: When models, data, context, users, regulations, incidents or observed performance materially change.

lessons.title: Designing a responsible AI workflow
objectives: Integrate evaluation and oversight into workflow design
Document an AI system use case transparently
lessons.teaching_material: A responsible workflow states what AI is allowed to do, what it is prohibited from doing, what evidence it may rely on, how outputs are evaluated and when a human must intervene. It includes a fallback when the model is unavailable or unreliable and records enough information to investigate mistakes. The goal is not maximum automation; it is a system in which automation creates value while human agency, accountability and safety remain visible and enforceable.
lessons.activity: Design the capstone AI workflow with task boundary, data boundary, prompt/process stages, evaluation set, human approvals, logging, fallback and incident-response plan.

self_check.q: Why include a fallback process?
self_check.a: The organization must still operate safely when the model fails, becomes unavailable or does not meet required confidence.

self_check.q: What should define the automation boundary?
self_check.a: The task's risk, evidence quality, reversibility, legal or institutional requirements and the ability of humans to oversee the result.

assessments.title: AI Output Verification Portfolio
assessments.instructions: Document three AI-assisted tasks with prompts, source boundaries, output checks, errors found and corrected final work. Include a short technical explanation of the AI task type, what the model can infer from patterns, and the limitations that require human verification.

assessments.title: AI Risk and Stakeholder Assessment
assessments.instructions: Evaluate one proposed AI use case for stakeholders, benefits, harms, bias, privacy, security, evidence and governance controls.

assessments.title: Responsible AI Workflow Capstone
assessments.instructions: Design and demonstrate a bounded AI workflow with an evaluation set, human oversight, data controls, audit log, fallback and incident-response procedure.
